mcqs.question: Why does a broadcast frame specifically (rather than a unicast frame) cause a network-wide storm on a looped topology with no loop prevention?
options: Broadcast frames are larger than unicast frames, so they saturate links faster
A switch always floods broadcast frames out every port by definition; with two paths between switches, that flooding loops forever and each pass duplicates the frame
Unicast frames are immune to loops because switches always know their destination
Broadcast frames use a different, more fragile physical encoding than unicast frames
mcqs.explanation: Broadcast frames are always flooded to every port by design, so with two redundant paths, that flooding has nowhere to stop and each circuit doubles the traffic — that's the storm. Frame size isn't the mechanism (option 1), unicast frames can also loop if their destination is unknown and gets flooded (option 3 overstates it), and there's no separate physical encoding for broadcast frames (option 4).

mcqs.question: In STP, why is a redundant port blocked rather than the cable itself being physically disconnected?
options: Physically disconnecting cables is not possible via software
Blocking is logical, not physical — the link stays up as a standby path so STP can quickly bring it back into forwarding state if the active path fails
Blocked ports still forward broadcast traffic, just not unicast traffic
STP always disconnects the cable; "blocking" is just informal terminology for a physical disconnect
mcqs.explanation: The whole value of STP is preserving the redundant path as a ready standby — blocking it logically (not physically) means it can be activated quickly if the primary path fails, which is the entire point of having redundancy in the first place. Blocked ports don't forward any traffic, broadcast or otherwise (option 3 false), and blocking is explicitly a logical state, not a physical disconnect (options 1 and 4 false).
